title: Names and Numbers
about: How website names get turned into the numbers computers use.

cards.prompt:
You type `example.com` into your [[browser]]. But [[routers|router]] deliver [[packets|packet]] using [[IP addresses|ip-address]], like `198.51.100.10`, and have no idea what "example.com" means.

So why do websites have names at all?

options.text: Routers need numbers, but people remember names more easily
Names make packets travel faster than plain numbers do
options.nudge: A name doesn't change how fast a packet moves. Think about who finds names easier: people or routers?

options.text: Names keep a website's IP address secret from hackers
options.nudge: Names don't hide anything: anyone can look up a website's address. Think about who finds names easier.

options.text: Names let your device skip the routers and go straight to the site
options.nudge: Every packet still travels through routers, and routers only read IP addresses. So who are the names really for?

cards.explanation: Every packet needs a destination **IP address**, because that's what routers use to deliver it. Names exist for people: `example.com` is far easier to remember than `198.51.100.10`. So before your browser can connect, something has to turn the name into an address.
cards.hint: Think about who uses names, and what routers need to deliver a packet.

cards.title: The internet's contacts app
cards.body:
A phone's contacts app works like this: you tap a **name**, and it finds the **number**.

The internet has the same thing, the **Domain Name System**, or **DNS**. Give it a name like `example.com`, and it gives back an [[IP address]] like `198.51.100.10`. That's a **DNS lookup**, and it happens before almost every connection you make.

cards.prompt: Match each part of the contacts-app idea to its internet version.
cards.explanation: The **name** is what people use, the **number** (IP address) is what the network uses, and **DNS** is the look-up service that connects the two. Once your device has the address, it can connect, just like a phone dials once it has the number.
cards.hint: Ask what each thing is used for: people remember the name, the [[network]] uses the number, and something looks one up from the other.
cards.nudge: Keep the two sides lined up by job: what you remember, what the network uses, the look-up service, and the step that happens once you have the number.

cards.prompt: Time for a real lookup. Run `nslookup example.com` to ask [[DNS]] for example.com's address (the top lines show who answered).
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Ask DNS for the address of example.com
commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.com
Address: 198.51.100.10
Name:	example.com
Address: 2001:db8::10

cards.explanation:
DNS answered with **two** addresses for example.com: an [[IPv4]] address, `198.51.100.10`, and an [[IPv6]] address, `2001:db8::10`. Your device can use either one.

The `Server` and `Address` lines at the very top aren't example.com. They show the DNS helper that answered your question.
cards.hint: Type the [[command]] exactly as it's shown in the prompt, then press Enter.
cards.nudge: Check the spelling and the space: the tool name comes first, then the website name.

cards.prompt:
A [[domain name|domain-name]] like `mail.example.org` is made of parts:

- `mail` is a **subdomain**: a name the owner chose to add.
- `org` is the **top-level domain** (**TLD**), shared by millions of names.
- `example` is the **domain** someone registered: `example.org`.

Names are read from **right to left**. Put the parts in order, from the **most general** at the top to the **most specific** at the bottom.
cards.explanation: Read right to left: the TLD `org` comes first, shared by millions of names. Then the domain `example`, making `example.org`, which one person or group registered. Last comes the subdomain `mail`, which the owner of example.org chose to add.
cards.hint: Start at the right-hand end of the name. Which part is shared by the most names?
cards.nudge: Reading left to right gives you the most specific part first. Flip it: the right-hand end is the most general.

cards.prompt: Whoever registers a domain can add any subdomains they like to its **left**. Who controls the name `login.example.com.example.org`?

options.nudge: That name appears in the middle, not at the end. What matters is the registered domain on the right-hand side.

options.text: Both owners share control of it
options.nudge: Only one domain is actually registered here. Read from the right to find it; the rest is just a subdomain.
The leftmost part is the most specific: a subdomain chosen by the owner. Look at the right-hand end instead.

cards.explanation: Read from the right: the TLD is `org` and the registered domain is `example.org`. Everything to its left, including `login.example.com`, is just a subdomain that **example.org's owner** chose to add. It says "example.com" in the middle, but the owner of example.com has nothing to do with it. Scammers use this trick to make links *look* like they belong to a site they don't.
cards.hint: Read from the right. Find the [[TLD]], then the registered domain next to it. Everything to its left is a [[subdomain]].

cards.prompt:
Some countries add an extra level. Many UK businesses register names ending in `.co.uk`: the TLD is `uk`, and `co.uk` is shared by millions of companies, a bit like `.com`.

Who controls `shop.example.co.uk`?

options.text: Whoever runs co.uk, since it sits next to the TLD
options.nudge: `co.uk` is shared by millions of companies, just like `.com`. It isn't one company's domain. Look one step further left.

options.text: The UK government, because the name ends in uk
options.nudge: A country code shows where a name is registered, not who runs the site. Look further left for the part someone registered.

options.text: Whoever owns the shop part at the start
options.nudge: The leftmost part is a subdomain, the most specific part. Its owner is whoever registered the domain to its right.

cards.explanation: Read from the right: `uk` is the TLD and `co.uk` is a shared ending, like `.com`. The first part after that, `example.co.uk`, is the domain someone registered, so **its owner** controls `shop.example.co.uk` and any other subdomain they add.
cards.hint: Use the right-to-left rule, as with `.com` names. Which part would one person or company actually have registered?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **DNS** turns names into [[IP addresses|ip-address]], like a contacts app.
- Names are read **right to left**: TLD, domain, then subdomains.
- A domain's owner controls every subdomain to its left.
